title: The Ark Comes Home
summary: After seven months of plague, the Philistines ask their priests and diviners how to return the ark. They send it back on a new cart pulled by two nursing cows whose calves have been penned up, with a guilt offering of five gold tumors and five gold rats. The cows go straight to Beth-shemesh, proving that the LORD sent the plague, and the Israelites there rejoice and offer sacrifices. But when some of the men look into the ark, the LORD strikes them, and the town sends the ark on to Kiriath-jearim.
story: Chapter 5 left the Philistine cities in panic, crying out to heaven and demanding that the ark be sent back. Chapter 6 tells how it gets home, and the return turns out to be as dangerous as the capture. The chapter closes the Philistine phase of the ark narrative and opens the question that the rest of the book will keep asking in different forms: who can stand before this holy God? The ark will sit at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years (7:2) until David brings it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6), which shows how long the loss of Shiloh shaped Israel's life.
historical:
Beth-shemesh was an Israelite town on the border with Philistine territory, in the Sorek Valley west of Jerusalem, and its name means house of the sun. It was assigned to the Levites in Joshua 21:16, which explains why Levites are on hand to lift down the ark. Excavations at Tel Beth-Shemesh show it was a border settlement in the Iron Age, with material culture distinct from the nearby Philistine cities. The wheat harvest in the valley points to late spring or early summer. Kiriath-jearim, where the ark goes next, lay higher in the hills to the northeast, on the road toward Jerusalem.

The number of those struck in verse 19 presents a textual problem. Most Hebrew manuscripts read seventy men, fifty thousand men, a strange phrase that many scholars regard as a scribal addition, since Beth-shemesh was a small town; several manuscripts and translations, including the BSB, read seventy. The ancient Greek translation also has a different wording of the first part of the verse, with a different explanation of why the men were struck.
cultural:
Isaiah 2:6 mentions diviners like the Philistines, and here the Philistines consult their priests and diviners about how to appease a foreign god. Their answer reflects common ancient practice. A guilt offering compensated a deity for an offense, and the golden images of tumors and rats function as offerings that represent the affliction itself, handed over to the god who sent it. Offering models of afflicted body parts at a healing shrine is known from later Greek sanctuaries, and the idea behind it was widespread. The five images match the five Philistine cities, so each city pays its share.

The test with the cows is ingenious. Nursing cows that had never been yoked would not naturally pull a cart in a straight line, and cows separated from their calves would instinctively turn back toward them. If they walked steadily away from their calves toward Israelite territory, lowing as they went, the diviners could be sure that the LORD was driving them. The Philistine reference to Pharaoh and Egypt shows how widely the exodus story had become known, and it casts them as people who have learned from history better than the Egyptians did.
literary: The chapter has two halves: the Philistines' careful plan for sending the ark back (verses 1-12) and Israel's mixed reception (verses 13-21). The first half has an almost comic tone, as the Philistines agonize over every detail and follow the cows to the border. The second half turns from joy to death. The chapter's last words echo chapter 5 in reverse: the Philistines asked what to do with the ark and sent it away, and now the men of Beth-shemesh ask a deeper question, “Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?” (verse 20), and they too send it away. The verb to return runs through the chapter eight times, marking the ark's movement home, but the story refuses to make the return simple.

outline.t: The Philistine priests' plan and test
The cows go straight to Beth-shemesh
Joy and sacrifice at Beth-shemesh; the five gold offerings
Death at Beth-shemesh, and the ark sent to Kiriath-jearim

doctrines.note: The ark's return shows that God's holiness is dangerous even for his own people when it is treated casually. The men of Beth-shemesh ask the right question, who can stand before this holy God, though they answer it by sending him away. The Law had warned that even the Levites who carried the holy things must not look at them (Numbers 4:20).

God guides the untrained cows straight home, overriding their instincts. The Philistines set a test to tell whether their suffering was chance or the LORD's hand, and God answers it plainly. Scripture presents him as governing even the details that people attribute to chance.

The Philistine priests tell their people to give glory to the God of Israel and not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh did. Pagans here show a better grasp of repentance than many in Israel, a theme the Prophets and Gospels also take up.

words.note: Asham, guilt offering, the term used in Leviticus 5 for an offering that makes restitution for a wrong done against the holy things of God. The Philistines use it here in a broader sense for compensation to an offended deity, but the use of Israel's own sacrificial term is striking: even outsiders recognize they owe the LORD reparation.

Tselem, image. It is the word used in Genesis 1 for humanity made in God's image, and elsewhere for idols and statues. Here it describes the golden models of tumors and rats. The Philistines give glory to the God of Israel through images, the very thing Israel was forbidden to make of him.

Akhbar, a mouse or rat, a small rodent. Rats are named for the first time here, though verse 5 says they were ravaging the land, which many take as a clue to the nature of the plague. The pairing of rats and swellings has led interpreters to suggest an outbreak of bubonic plague, though the text doesn't say.

Shuv, to return or turn back. It is one of the most important verbs in the Old Testament, used both for physical return and for repentance (turning back to God). In this chapter it describes the ark's return and the Philistines' desire to send it back, and in chapter 7 it will be used of Israel turning back to the LORD.

christ: The chapter's closing question, who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?, is one the whole Bible asks. Psalm 24 asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD and answers that it is the one with clean hands and a pure heart. The New Testament answers the question by pointing to Christ, who is holy and who brings people into God's presence. Hebrews 10:19-22 speaks of believers entering the most holy place with confidence through the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way. The connection is thematic rather than predictive: 1 Samuel 6 does not foretell Christ, but it raises in stark form the problem of sinful people living near a holy God, which the gospel claims to answer.

hard.q: Why did God strike down the men of Beth-shemesh, who were Israelites rejoicing at the ark's return?
hard.a: The judgment feels disproportionate: people who welcomed the ark with joy and sacrifice are killed for looking into it. The text's explanation is that they looked inside the ark, treating the most holy object in Israel as something to be inspected. Israel's law had set strict boundaries around the ark; even the Levites were not to see the holy things uncovered, or they would die (Numbers 4:20). Beth-shemesh was a Levitical town, so its people had less excuse than the Philistines. Some scholars prefer the ancient Greek text, which gives a different reason (that some did not rejoice), and think the Hebrew has suffered in transmission. Others read the story as a sober lesson: God's presence is not safe to handle casually, even for his own people. The same lesson recurs when Uzzah dies touching the ark in 2 Samuel 6. On any reading, the chapter wants readers to feel the danger as well as the joy of God's nearness.

questions: The Philistines treated their suffering as a sign to take God seriously. How do people today tend to interpret hardship, and when might it be a call to turn toward God?
The men of Beth-shemesh rejoiced at the ark and then treated it carelessly. How can familiarity with holy things lead to carelessness?
“Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?” How would you answer that question?
